Day 61 of 100 · Docker

Why Containers

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityDockerPublished journey entry

Containers package an application with its userspace dependencies while isolating processes on a shared host kernel, reducing environment drift without pretending each workload is a virtual machine.

Architecture / mental model

application + userspace dependencies → image → container namespaces/cgroups → shared host kernel

How it works

An application can fail even when its source code did not change because the runtime environment changed: library versions, system packages, configuration or filesystem assumptions drifted.

A container image packages the userspace filesystem and application dependencies into a repeatable artifact. A running container adds process, network and mount isolation around that image.

The efficiency difference from a virtual machine is fundamental: containers normally share the host kernel instead of booting a guest kernel for every workload. Namespaces isolate views of processes, networking, mounts, hostname and IPC while cgroups can constrain resources.

Hands-on reference

docker version
docker run --rm alpine:latest uname -a
docker run --rm alpine:latest cat /etc/os-release

Verification

Compare the userspace distribution reported inside the container with the host while observing that the running container uses the host kernel family. Inspect namespace/process isolation with `docker inspect` and host process tools.

Field note / gotcha

A container is not a tiny VM. The shared-kernel model is both a major efficiency advantage and part of the security boundary you must understand.

Security considerations

Use trusted/minimal images, keep the host kernel patched and avoid granting containers unnecessary host namespaces, devices or privileges.

What I learned

Containers solve packaging and isolation problems; they do not erase the host or its kernel.
